title: norway offers case study us financial gravity 2026 09 04
author: Liam Proud
text:
LONDON, Sept 4 (Reuters Breakingviews) - The only thing more dangerous than being over-exposed to American assets is being under-exposed. That's one way to understand a couple
, opens new tab
 of letters
, opens new tab
 written to the Norwegian Ministry of Finance this week by the manager ​of the country's $2.3 trillion sovereign-wealth fund.
Norges Bank Investment Management, run by former hedge fund impresario Nicolai Tangen, was responding to questions raised earlier ‌this year by the government concerning geopolitical and concentration risks, and the specifics of its bond investment strategy. The fund's proposed changes involve a material shift away from U.S. government debt, which would go down from about a third of the overall fixed-income benchmark index to just over a fifth.
Since fixed-income more broadly is supposed to be 30% of the fund, this change would imply that Treasuries shrink ​to about 7% of the whole investment portfolio over time, compared with 10% now. The gap is currently equivalent to roughly $86 billion.
Yet the proposed move has ​nothing to do with geopolitics or worries about U.S. financial hegemony. In fact, the tweaks would leave exposure to the greenback ⁠almost unchanged at 53%. Tangen's team is proposing substituting direct U.S. Treasury-bond investments for American state-backed mortgage-backed securities. Norges points out that bonds linked to home loans come with ​similar credit risk but lower volatility and higher returns.
The fund explicitly addresses geopolitical risk and the dangers of U.S. equity concentration in one of the letters. Its modelling suggests ​that, using constant price-earnings ratios, the so-called Magnificent Seven and other American technology groups could account for 50% of the value of the MSCI All-Country World Index in a decade, up from roughly a third right now.
The question is what, if anything, to do about this. The right answer is probably nothing, for two reasons. First, reducing concentration would involve introducing capped exposure to the biggest and ​fastest-growing companies. One possible rule could be that no company can make up more than, say, 2% of the total equity portfolio.
That may hurt returns. Nvidia (NVDA.O)
, opens new tab
 and Apple (AAPL.O)
, opens new tab
, ​which at the half-year point together accounted for roughly 5% of Norges Bank's entire fund, are big for a reason. They generate a lot of earnings, and investors expect them to keep ‌doing so. Tangen's ⁠team studied the effects of limiting how much a fund could concentrate its bets in individual stocks would have helped or hurt its performance since 1994. The answer? Limiting exposure always hurt returns: capped-concentration portfolios trailed the roughly 9% annualised total return of the uncapped one.
Second, explicitly trying to minimise geographic concentration would risk making Norges Bank look like a political actor. The fund doesn't quite say this, stating instead that it is important that the financial objective remains firm "and is perceived as such by the outside world". ​But the subtext is clear. Dumping U.S. ​or Chinese assets en masse could make ⁠Norges Bank seem like fair game for reprisals if things got truly messy in a future trade war. The letter mentions increased taxation, regulatory intervention and even confiscation as extreme tail risks. In other words, trying to manage geopolitical risks can paradoxically have ​the effect of increasing them.
